notes.meaning: Eliashib the high priest and the other priests started the building project at the Sheep Gate on the northeast side of the city. Sheep meant for temple sacrifices were brought through this gate, so the priests set it apart for God by dedicating it with prayer. They also rebuilt two strong military towers nearby, called the Tower of the Hundred and the Tower of Hananel. Spiritual leaders gave a good example to the whole community by getting their own hands dirty first.

Workers from the town of Jericho took the next stretch of wall, and Zaccur son of Imri built right beside them. Even though Jericho was located miles away down in the Jordan Valley, its people came willingly to help Jerusalem. Dividing the wall into small sections helped everyone work side by side at the exact same time.

The family of Hassenaah rebuilt the Fish Gate on the northern wall of Jerusalem. This entrance was named for the market nearby where traders brought in sea fish and fish from the Jordan River. The builders did not just fix the stone opening, but also set heavy timber beams, doors, locks, and crossbars in place so the city could be locked tight.

Three more men and their helpers took the next three sections: Meremoth, Meshullam, and Zadok. These parts of the wall were not entirely knocked down, so these builders strengthened the weak spots and filled the gaps. Meremoth was a faithful priest who later took on an extra section of wall as well.

The common people from the town of Tekoa built the next stretch, but their rich leaders refused to help. These proud nobles acted like stubborn oxen that would not bend their necks to a wooden yoke. Even so, the ordinary citizens ignored the bad example of their rulers and gladly served the Lord.

Joiada and Meshullam repaired the Jeshanah Gate, often called the Old Gate, on the northwest side of Jerusalem. Like the builders of the Fish Gate, they finished the whole gate by setting up wooden beams, heavy doors, metal bolts, and crossbars. Their careful work helped protect the older quarter of the city from northern invaders.

Melatiah from Gibeon, Jadon from Meronoth, and men from the towns of Gibeon and Mizpah repaired the next section. These towns lay several miles north of Jerusalem in the territory of Benjamin. They worked all the way to the official seat or residence used by the Persian governor when he visited the area west of the Euphrates River.

Uzziel, who worked with gold, and Hananiah, who made perfumes and spices, repaired the next part of the wall. Although they worked in skilled crafts rather than heavy construction, they gladly volunteered for hard labor. They strengthened the defenses all the way to the Broad Wall, a thick section of older wall that had survived destruction.

Rephaiah son of Hur repaired the next piece of wall. He served as the governor over half of the district of Jerusalem. Even as an important civic leader, he was ready to put his own energy into manual labor for the good of his people.

Jedaiah son of Harumaph repaired the section of wall directly across from his own home, and Hattush repaired the space next to him. Nehemiah wisely asked residents to build near their own houses because they had a natural interest in making that part strong and safe. This arrangement also kept workers from wasting time traveling across town.

Malchijah and Hasshub repaired a second section along with the Tower of the Ovens on the western wall. This tower stood near public ovens that were likely used for baking bread or firing pottery clay. Malchijah had previously confessed sin in the days of Ezra, showing that a person with past failures can still serve God faithfully.

Shallum, the ruler of Jerusalem's other half-district, repaired the next section with the help of his daughters. These women likely paid for workers or took an active part in the construction work themselves. Their willingness shows that building God's community was a team effort for everyone in the family.

Hanun and the citizens of Zanoah repaired the Valley Gate on the southwest corner of the city. They hung its doors, set its bolts and bars, and repaired a long stretch of wall measuring one thousand cubits, or about fifteen hundred feet. This was a huge section, likely because that part of the ridge had suffered less damage from enemy attacks.

Malchijah son of Rechab, governor of the Beth-haccherem district, repaired the Dung Gate on the southern side of the city. Trash and temple waste were carried out through this gate into the valley below. Malchijah took on this humble and unpleasant post, completely rebuilding the entrance and securing it with doors, bolts, and bars.

Shallun, the leader of the Mizpah district, rebuilt the Fountain Gate near the southeast corner of Jerusalem. He added a roof to shelter the gate, hung its doors, and installed its locks and bars. He also fixed the wall around the Pool of Siloam near the royal gardens, all the way to the stone stairs coming down from the City of David.

A different Nehemiah, the son of Azbuk and ruler of half the Beth-zur district, repaired the next stretch of the eastern wall. His work extended past the royal burial caves of King David's family, the artificial water reservoir built in Hezekiah's day, and the barracks known as the House of the Mighty. This line ran along the steep rocky cliffs of Mount Zion.

A group of Levites rebuilt the next section under the direction of Rehum son of Bani. Right next to them, Hashabiah, ruler of half the Keilah district, oversaw repairs on behalf of his own region. These leaders made sure temple helpers and local citizens carried their fair share of the burden.

The people from the second half of Keilah completed the next section under their ruler, Binnui son of Henadad. Having both leaders of Keilah present meant that their whole hometown was united in the work. When neighbors cooperate with each other, large projects get finished much faster.

Ezer son of Jeshua, another leader from Mizpah, repaired a second stretch of wall near the armory. This section stood at a sharp turn in the wall where weapons and armor were stored for the city guards. Securing this corner was vital because enemy soldiers often attacked wall angles first.

Baruch son of Zabbai worked with special enthusiasm to repair the next section from the corner up to the entrance of Eliashib the high priest's house. The text singles him out for his burning zeal and eager pace. His energetic spirit likely inspired the other workers around him to pick up their speed.

Meremoth son of Uriah repaired a second section of wall, running from the front door of Eliashib's large house to the far end of the property. He had already finished his first assigned portion earlier along the north wall. Meremoth did not quit when his first job was done, but gladly stepped in to do extra work.

Priests who lived in the surrounding countryside and Jordan Valley repaired the next stretch of the wall. Even though their regular homes were outside Jerusalem near Jericho, they came to the city to protect God's dwelling place. They saw the safety of the temple city as their personal responsibility.

Benjamin and Hasshub made repairs right in front of their home, and Azariah repaired the section beside his own house. Once again, families were assigned to the wall bordering their own property. People naturally put their best effort into building walls that keep their own loved ones safe.

Binnui son of Henadad took on a second assignment, repairing from Azariah's house to the bend and corner of the wall. This turn marked the northeast angle of the ancient City of David. Binnui showed great commitment by tackling this tricky turn in the masonry.

Palal worked across from the corner near the tall lookout tower projecting from the upper royal palace by the courtyard of the prison. Next to him, Pedaiah son of Parosh continued the repairs. Jeremiah the prophet had once been held in this prison court during the Babylonian siege years before.

The temple assistants, called the Nethinim, lived on the hill of Ophel just south of the temple courts. They helped repair the section opposite the Water Gate to the east and its lookout tower. Living by the Water Gate made practical sense because one of their main jobs was carrying fresh water up for temple ceremonies.

The common men of Tekoa stepped forward to build a second section, running from the large projecting tower to the wall of Ophel. Even though their rich nobles had refused to do any work at all, these ordinary citizens willingly doubled their labor. God honors humble workers who do more than is asked of them.

Priests repaired the wall above the Horse Gate, with each priest working directly in front of his own residence. This gate stood between the palace and temple, near where war horses were kept and led out to drink from the Kidron Brook. These religious servants did their duty by protecting their own doorsteps.

Zadok son of Immer repaired the wall opposite his home, and Shemaiah the guard of the East Gate repaired the next part. Shemaiah guarded the sacred entrance to the temple courts, which had stayed closed while the city was open. He set aside his own comfort to help build public walls for everyone else.

Hananiah and Hanun, the sixth son of Zalaph, repaired another section of wall. Hanun joined the work even though his five older brothers apparently sat it out. Beside them, Meshullam repaired the wall opposite his single rented room, proving that a person does not need wealth or a grand mansion to serve the Lord.

Malchijah, a craftsman from the goldsmiths' guild, made repairs up to the house of the temple servants and merchants near the Inspection Gate. This gate led to a public gathering area where soldiers or offerings were inspected. Skillful tradesmen laid heavy stones alongside everyone else to keep God's city safe.

Goldsmiths and merchants repaired the final section between the upper corner room and the Sheep Gate. This brought the construction loop all the way back to the very place where the priests had started in verse one. By working together shoulder to shoulder, ordinary people finished the entire protective circle around Jerusalem.
